config.title: Build notes CRUD REST API

intro.title: Build notes CRUD REST API
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a RESTful API for a simple notes application using Node.js. You will learn to implement CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations to manage notes. The core programming concepts involve handling HTTP requests, routing, and working with in-memory data storage. You'll use core Node.js modules like `http` and `fs` to create endpoints and manage data persistence. By the end, you'll have a functional API that can create, retrieve, update, and delete notes through standard HTTP methods.
intro.usecase: A REST API for notes is the backend engine for countless productivity and collaboration applications. Developers build these APIs to power features like note creation in apps like Evernote, task updates in project management tools like Asana, and data synchronization in mobile note-taking apps. Implementing CRUD operations allows users to create new notes, read their existing lists, edit content, and delete items—core interactions in any digital workspace. Mastering this pattern is essential for building scalable, data-driven web services that handle user-generated content securely and efficiently.

objectives: Initialize a Node.js project with Express framework for building a REST API
Configure Express middleware to handle JSON request bodies and route requests
Implement GET endpoints to retrieve all notes and specific notes by ID
Construct POST endpoints to create new notes with validation
Manipulate data by implementing PUT endpoints to update existing notes
Control data deletion by implementing DELETE endpoints to remove notes
Integrate error handling for invalid requests and missing resources

steps.title: Import Express and create Express app
steps.instruction: Import the Express framework using require() and create an Express application instance.
steps.hint: Use require('express') to import Express, then call express() to create an app instance.
steps.seedCode: // Import Express and create an Express app instance
steps.expectedOutcome: The Express module is imported and an app instance is created, ready for configuration.
successCriteria: Express is imported using require() and an Express application instance is created.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've both imported Express using require() and created an app instance by calling express().
steps.feedbackWrong: import Express using require('express') and create an app instance with express().

steps.title: Add middleware for JSON parsing
steps.instruction: Add the express.json() middleware to your Express app so it can automatically parse JSON request bodies.
steps.hint: Use app.use() with express.json() as the argument to add this middleware.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding middleware to an Express app
app.use(express.json());

// Import Express and create an Express app instance


// Add JSON parsing middleware here
steps.expectedOutcome: Your Express app will be configured to parse incoming JSON data from request bodies.
successCriteria: The app.use(express.json()) middleware is added to the Express app.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using app.use() with express.json() as shown in the example.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to use app.use(express.json()) to add JSON parsing middleware.

steps.title: Initialize in-memory notes array
steps.instruction: Create a variable named 'notes' and initialize it as an empty array. This array will store note objects.
steps.hint: Use 'let' or 'const' to declare the variable, then assign it an empty array [].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing an array for tasks
let tasks = [];
steps.expectedOutcome: A variable 'notes' is declared and set to an empty array.
successCriteria: The 'notes' variable is declared and initialized as an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared a variable named 'notes' and set it to an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to create a variable called 'notes' and initialize it as an empty array.

steps.title: Create GET /notes endpoint
steps.instruction: Add a GET route at '/notes' that returns all notes from the in-memory array as JSON.
steps.hint: Use app.get() with the path '/notes' and a handler function that sends the notes array using res.json().
steps.expectedOutcome: A GET endpoint at '/notes' that responds with the notes array in JSON format.
successCriteria: The code includes app.get('/notes', handler) that sends the notes array as JSON response.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your route uses app.get('/notes', ...) and sends the notes array with res.json(notes).
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax: you need to define a GET route at '/notes' that returns the notes array as JSON.

steps.title: Create POST /notes endpoint
steps.instruction: Add a POST route at '/notes' that creates a new note with auto-generated ID and adds it to the array. Use app.post() to define the route.
steps.hint: Inside the route handler, generate a unique ID for the new note (e.g., using Date.now()), extract the note data from req.body, and push the new note object into the notes array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A POST route at '/notes' is defined that creates a new note with an auto-generated ID, adds it to the notes array, and returns the created note with a 201 status.
successCriteria: The POST route is defined with app.post('/notes', handler). The handler generates an ID, creates a note object from req.body, pushes it to notes, and sends a response with status 201 and the new note.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your route handler generates an ID, creates the note object, adds it to the array, and sends a proper response.
steps.feedbackWrong: The POST endpoint is not correctly implemented. Review the example and ensure you're using app.post() with the correct path and handler logic.

steps.title: Create GET /notes/:id endpoint
steps.instruction: Add a GET route at '/notes/:id' that finds and returns a single note by ID parameter.
steps.hint: Use app.get() with '/notes/:id' as the path. Access the id parameter from req.params.id. Find the note in the notes array using find() method. Return the note with res.json() if found, otherwise return a 404 status with a message.
steps.expectedOutcome: A GET route at '/notes/:id' is implemented that retrieves a specific note by ID and returns it, or returns a 404 if not found.
successCriteria: The route uses app.get() with '/notes/:id', accesses req.params.id, finds the note using find(), returns the note with res.json() if found, and returns a 404 status with a message if not found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your route handles both cases: returning the note if found and a 404 response if not found.
steps.feedbackWrong: The endpoint isn't working as expected. Check that you're using the correct path, accessing the id parameter properly, and handling both success and error cases.

steps.title: Add error handling for GET /notes/:id
steps.instruction: In the existing GET /notes/:id endpoint, add logic to return a 404 status with a JSON error message when the requested note ID is not found in the notes array.
steps.hint: After finding the note with find(), check if it exists. If not, use res.status(404).json() to send an error response.
steps.expectedOutcome: The endpoint now properly handles missing notes by returning a 404 status with an error message, preventing crashes and providing a clear API response.
successCriteria: The GET /notes/:id endpoint includes a conditional check for a missing note and returns res.status(404).json() with an error object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to include both the status(404) and json() call with an error message. Check your conditional logic.
steps.feedbackWrong: The endpoint still returns the note directly without checking if it exists. Add an if statement to handle the case where note is undefined.

steps.title: Create PUT /notes/:id endpoint
steps.instruction: Add a PUT route at '/notes/:id' that updates the title and content of an existing note. Place it after the existing GET /notes/:id route.
steps.hint: Use app.put() with the same route pattern as GET /notes/:id. Find the note by id, update its properties from req.body, and return the updated note.
steps.expectedOutcome: A PUT route is added that can update existing notes by ID.
successCriteria: The PUT route is defined at '/notes/:id', finds the note by id, updates title and content from req.body, and returns the updated note.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your route correctly updates the note's title and content.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PUT endpoint is missing or incorrect. Make sure to use app.put() with the correct route and update logic.

steps.title: Add error handling for PUT /notes/:id
steps.instruction: Inside the PUT /notes/:id endpoint, add a check to return a 404 status with a JSON error message when trying to update a note that doesn't exist.
steps.hint: After finding the note index, check if it's -1 (not found) and return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Note not found' }).
steps.expectedOutcome: The PUT endpoint will now properly handle requests for non-existent notes by returning a 404 status with an error message.
successCriteria: The PUT /notes/:id endpoint includes a conditional check that returns res.status(404).json({ error: 'Note not found' }) when the note index is -1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking if noteIndex equals -1 and returning the 404 response before attempting to update the note.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PUT endpoint still doesn't handle non-existent notes. Add a conditional check after finding the note index to return a 404 response when the index is -1.

steps.title: Create DELETE /notes/:id endpoint
steps.instruction: Add a DELETE route at '/notes/:id' that removes a note from the notes array by ID.
steps.hint: Use app.delete() with the route path and a callback that finds the note index and removes it using splice.
steps.expectedOutcome: A DELETE route is added that removes a note from the array and sends a 204 No Content response.
successCriteria: The DELETE route is defined at '/notes/:id', finds the note index, removes it from the array, and sends a 204 response.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your DELETE route removes the note from the array and sends a 204 response.
steps.feedbackWrong: The DELETE endpoint is missing or incorrect. Check the route path and the logic to find and remove the note.

steps.title: Add error handling for DELETE /notes/:id
steps.instruction: In the DELETE /notes/:id endpoint, add a conditional check to return a 404 status with a JSON error message when the note to delete is not found in the notes array.
steps.hint: Use an if statement to check if noteIndex is -1 (meaning not found), then return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Note not found' }).
steps.expectedOutcome: The DELETE endpoint now properly handles cases where the requested note ID does not exist by returning a 404 status with an error message.
successCriteria: The DELETE /notes/:id endpoint includes an if statement that checks if noteIndex is -1 and returns res.status(404).json({ error: 'Note not found' }) when true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the error handling might be incomplete. Make sure you have an if statement checking if noteIndex is -1 and return a 404 status with a JSON error object before proceeding with the deletion.
steps.feedbackWrong: The DELETE endpoint doesn't have the required error handling. You need to add a conditional check for when the note isn't found and return a 404 response with an error message.

steps.title: Start the Express server
steps.instruction: Add app.listen() to start the server on port 3000.
steps.hint: Use app.listen() with port 3000 and a callback function that logs a message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will start and listen for requests on port 3000.
successCriteria: app.listen() is called with port 3000 and a callback that logs a message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added app.listen(), but make sure to include port 3000 and a callback that logs a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server isn't started yet. Use app.listen() with port 3000 and a callback.
